idiom_name: typed strategy interface over the host's primitives (LockManager via lib.dom, Atomics in workers)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not a runtime: the available strategies are the host's - navigator.locks, typed in lib.dom.d.ts as readonly locks: LockManager, and worker-level Atomics over SharedArrayBuffer - and because types are erased, a policy cannot be enforced at run time and a missing lock remains a data-flow problem. Where a project does want a swappable policy, TypeScript expresses it as a higher-order interface (interface LockStrategy { run<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> }) with implementations for a serializing queue, a no-op or a Web Locks-backed lock; the abstract Lock class plus guard of the classic pattern buys nothing over that single function. As in JavaScript, prefer one owning task per resource over mutual exclusion for ordinary async code, and reach for the typed LockManager only for resources genuinely shared across workers or tabs.
pitfalls: Type-only policies vanish at compile time: nothing prevents a call path from bypassing the interface, so exclusion stays a discipline or lint rule rather than a guarantee.
lib.dom's LockManager is ambient - a Node-only build without the DOM lib has no declaration for it, and including the DOM lib to type a lock drags in every other browser global.

A class holding a promise queue serializes per instance only: two instances or two bundles of the same module do not share it, so per-resource exclusion needs a module-level or explicitly shared strategy object.
alternative: Express exclusion as a typed higher-order function (one serializing promise queue per resource) and rely on message passing between workers; type navigator.locks (LockManager) only for resources that are genuinely shared across workers or tabs.
